title: Not one of us (Mark 9:38–41)
hook: whoever is not against us is for us

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was diakonos, the one who waits on tables, and he stood a child in the middle. Your line was last of all, servant of all.

The right jersey. The right school. The group chat you were or weren't added to. Groups have unofficial rules about who's in. Now, just after the lesson about the child, John speaks up. Mark has told us Jesus nicknamed him and his brother the sons of thunder. He seems pleased with his news. In the King James Bible: "Master, we saw one casting out devils in thy name, and he followeth not us: and we forbad him, because he followeth not us." A stranger, doing good in the name of Jesus, and they shut him down. Listen to the reason, twice over. Not: he doesn't follow you. He doesn't follow us.
screen: `WHO'S IN THE GROUP?` → `A STRANGER, USING THE NAME.` → `HE FOLLOWETH NOT US.`

segments.voice: Jesus answers in three short words: "Forbid him not." Nobody who does a mighty work in my name, he says, can turn around the next moment and speak evil of me. Then the line: "For he that is not against us is on our part." The circle is wider than John drew it. And he sets the bar lower still: whoever gives you a cup of water to drink in my name, because you belong to Christ, will not lose their reward. A cup of water. The Hebrew Bible has a scene like this. In the book of Numbers, two men named Eldad and Medad start prophesying in the camp without having been at the official gathering, and young Joshua begs Moses to stop them. Moses says, in effect: I wish all the Lord's people were prophets. To be fair, the Gospels also keep a saying that sounds like the opposite. In Matthew, Jesus says whoever is not with me is against me. Christians keep both. Some read Matthew's as about where a person stands toward Jesus himself, and today's as about how his followers treat people outside their own circle. Churches today differ, and argue about real things. Some also set aside a yearly week to pray for Christian unity, side by side. The disciples asked who's with us. His answer was who's for us.
screen: `FORBID HIM NOT.` · `NOT AGAINST US IS FOR US.` · `A CUP OF WATER IS ENOUGH.` · `MOSES: WOULD THAT ALL WERE PROPHETS.` · then, large: `HE THAT IS NOT AGAINST US IS ON OUR PART.`

segments.voice: Think of someone outside your circle who does good: a person from a different church, or a different way of being Christian than the one you know best, the neighbor who runs the food drive, the nurse, the church down the road that worships in a way you don't. Name one good thing they do, and mean it. If you pray, thank God for them by name; if you don't, just say thank you in your head.
John, the one who tried to stop a stranger casting out demons in Jesus's name. What Jesus answered: forbid him not.
Your line: not against us, for us. Even a cup of water counts. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some churches take part in a yearly Week of Prayer for Christian Unity, when Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant congregations pray together or visit one another.

fork.setup: you're John. you've seen a stranger healing people in Jesus's name, and you've told him to stop. how does Jesus react?
options: he thanks you for protecting the group.
he tells you not to stop him.
he goes to find the man himself.
fork.reveal: "Forbid him not." the circle is wider than John drew it. even a cup of water, given in his name, counts.

trapdoor: what you thought: be nice to outsiders.
what it means: the disciples drew the line at their own group; Jesus drew it at who is working for good in his name.
what a scholar hears: an echo of Numbers 11, Eldad and Medad, and Moses refusing to silence them. Matthew 12:30 keeps the opposite-sounding saying.

notes: The distinction offered between Matthew 12:30 and Mark 9:40 is one common harmonizing reading, attributed to 'many'. Confirm fairness.
Week of Prayer for Christian Unity (traditionally January 18–25 in the northern hemisphere) is mentioned without a date in the script; confirm that this passage is 'often' read.
'Thousands of churches' refers to denominations worldwide; the figure is loose on purpose. Confirm.
Original-language game left null: no single original word carries this day.
